walkthrough:
What Is Built Into the Stick**
Think of the pad at the end as a tiny dry laboratory. Two enzymes are immobilised in the pad: glucose oxidase and peroxidase. Immobilised means held in place so they do not wash away but can still react instantly when urine wets the pad.

First Reaction - Making a Signal Molecule**
When you dip the stick in urine, any glucose present meets glucose oxidase. This enzyme catalyses oxidation of glucose using oxygen to form gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide. Hydrogen peroxide is the key intermediate - it carries the message that glucose was present.

Second Reaction - Turning Signal Into Colour**
Hydrogen peroxide itself is colourless, so peroxidase uses it to oxidise a colourless chromogen dye precursor in the same pad. The oxidised chromogen becomes coloured. So colourless to coloured is the visible colour change, for example yellow to green-brown depending on brand.

Reading the Result**
You compare the pad colour after the stated time with a printed colour chart on the container. The chart is semi-quantitative. A darker / more intense colour means higher urine glucose concentration. The test is specific for glucose and does not give an exact numerical blood glucose value at that moment.

Final answer: Pad contains immobilised enzymes: glucose oxidase and peroxidase. Stick dipped in urine / urinated on. Glucose oxidised to give hydrogen peroxide. Hydrogen peroxide reacts with colourless chromogen / dye, catalysed by peroxidase, to give coloured product / colour change. Compare colour with colour chart. More glucose gives darker colour. Specific for glucose only. Does not give numerical current blood glucose concentration.

Finish the loop - what type of control system brings the level back to normal and then switches off the response?
walkthrough:
Detecting High Blood Glucose**
Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas act as sensors. When blood glucose rises above normal, for example after a meal, beta cells detect this and secrete more insulin directly into the blood.

Getting Glucose Into Cells**
Insulin travels in blood to liver, muscle and fat. In the liver it increases glucose uptake and phosphorylation to trap glucose inside. In muscle and fat cells it causes more GLUT4 channel proteins to be added to the cell surface membrane, greatly increasing permeability to glucose so glucose diffuses in.

Using Up and Storing Glucose**
Inside cells, insulin increases the rate of respiration so more glucose is broken down for ATP. In liver and muscle it also stimulates glycogenesis, conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage. At the same time it inhibits glucagon secretion and so decreases gluconeogenesis, formation of new glucose.

Switching Off by Negative Feedback**
As these effects remove glucose from blood, blood glucose concentration falls back toward normal. The beta cells detect the fall and reduce insulin secretion. That is negative feedback - the response reverses the original rise and restores the set point.

Final answer: High glucose detected by beta cells in islets of Langerhans in pancreas. More insulin secreted into blood. Increases glucose uptake by liver; increases permeability to glucose in muscle and fat cells by addition of GLUT4 to membranes. Increases rate of respiration of glucose. Stimulates conversion of glucose to glycogen / glycogenesis. Inhibits glucagon secretion / decreases gluconeogenesis. Negative feedback restores normal.
